title: THEY CALLED THEM GODS—AND PAUL RAN INTO THE CROWD HORRIFIED
paragraphs: THEY CALLED THEM GODS—AND PAUL RAN INTO THE CROWD HORRIFIED
The terrifying moment Paul and Barnabas were offered worship—and why their response exposes something the modern Christian world desperately needs to remember.
There is a kind of applause that should terrify a servant of Jesus.
Not criticism.
Not rejection.
Applause.
Because rejection can drive you to your knees.
But admiration can quietly tempt you onto a throne that never belonged to you.
Paul had just watched something extraordinary happen.
In Lystra sat a man whose feet had never carried him anywhere.
Luke does not describe him as someone recovering from an injury. Acts 14:8 says he was unable to use his feet, “lame from birth,” and had never walked.
Imagine living your entire life watching everybody else go somewhere.
Children running.
Workers leaving for the day.
Families walking home.
People entering rooms without thinking about the miracle hidden inside an ordinary step.
And you remain there.
Then Paul looks at him.
Paul sees that the man has faith to be healed and cries out:
“Stand upright on your feet.”
And the impossible happens.
The man springs up.
He walks.
Acts 14:10 uses the Greek verb ἥλατο — hēlato, meaning that he leaped or sprang up.
The man who had never taken a normal first step suddenly leaped.
Can you imagine the sound of that crowd?
Someone who had probably been part of the scenery of their city for years was standing.
Walking.
Moving.
Alive with a freedom his body had never known.
And that is when a beautiful miracle became a dangerous misunderstanding.
The people began shouting in their own Lycaonian language:
“The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!”
They called Barnabas Zeus.
They called Paul Hermes because Paul was the chief speaker.
Then the priest of Zeus arrived with bulls and garlands.
This was no metaphor.
No exaggerated compliment.
No ancient version of saying, “You guys are amazing.”
They were preparing a sacrifice.
The crowd had witnessed the power of the living God…
and tried to give His glory to the servants standing nearby.

Then Paul and Barnabas did something that should make every Christian leader, preacher, worship singer, ministry creator, influencer, teacher—and every believer who has ever secretly enjoyed being spiritually admired—uncomfortable.
They did not accept the honor.
They did not smile and say, “Well, technically, God did it through us.”
They did not allow the ceremony to continue because it gave them a larger platform.
They did not reason that accepting a little misplaced admiration might help them reach more people later.
They tore their clothes.
Acts 14:14 says:
διαρρήξαντες τὰ ἱμάτια ἑαυτῶν — diarrēxantes ta himatia heautōn
They tore their own garments.
Then they rushed into the crowd crying out.
Picture that.
People are trying to worship you…
and you are running toward them begging them to stop.
Paul and Barnabas understood something frightening:
There are moments when receiving what people desperately want to give you would actually rob God of what belongs to Him.
And perhaps the most revealing words come next.
They cried:
“Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you.”
The Greek expression is:
ὁμοιοπαθεῖς ἐσμεν ὑμῖν — homoiopatheis esmen hymin
“We are of the same nature as you.”
Human.
Mortal.
Dependent.
Not gods.
Not saviors.
Not the source.
They were essentially saying:
Stop looking at us as though the power came from us.
And then Paul redirects their attention toward the One who deserves it:
“…that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them.”
That sentence changes everything.
Because Paul was not merely rejecting worship.
He was redirecting worship.
Away from the creature.
Toward the Creator.
Away from dead idols.
Toward the living God.
Away from Paul.
Toward God.
And that is where this ancient scene becomes painfully modern.
Because we may no longer arrive with bulls and garlands.
But human beings have not stopped building altars.
We simply learned how to disguise them.
Followers.
Views.
Platforms.
Celebrity pastors.
Political personalities.
Christian influencers.
Favorite theologians.
Worship leaders.
Authors.
Miracle workers.
Denominations.
Ministries.
Even the person whose sermons helped you survive your darkest season.
God absolutely uses people.
Paul himself would later tell believers to imitate him as he imitated Christ.
But a messenger is not the Messiah.
A vessel is not the Fountain.
A preacher can tell you about forgiveness.
He cannot forgive your sins in God's place.
A teacher can explain the cross.
She did not die on it for you.
A worship leader can lead you into a song about Jesus.
That singer is not Jesus.
A ministry can help nourish your faith.
That ministry is not your Savior.
And perhaps some of us need to hear this even more personally.
Sometimes we are not tempted to worship another person.
Sometimes we are tempted to become the person everybody worships.
We want to be needed.
Recognized.
Quoted.
Praised.
Followed.
Thanked.
We tell ourselves we only want God to receive the glory…
but then someone else gets the recognition and something inside us hurts.
That little wound may reveal more than we want to admit.
Would you still serve if nobody knew your name?
Would you still give if nobody publicly thanked you?
Would you still preach if somebody else received the applause?
Would you still obey Jesus if your obedience never became content?
Would you still pray in the secret place if there were no camera there to record your tears?
Would you still love Christ if following Him made you smaller instead of famous?
Paul and Barnabas were confronted with one of ministry's most intoxicating temptations:
People wanted to make them bigger than they were.
And they refused.
But the story gets even more unsettling.
The same city that wanted to worship Paul would soon participate in brutal violence against him.
Acts 14:19 tells us that opponents arrived, persuaded the crowds, and Paul was stoned and dragged outside the city because they thought he was dead.
Do not miss the emotional whiplash.
One moment:
“The gods have come down!”
Soon afterward:
Drag his body outside the city.
That is the crowd.
Hosanna can become crucify.
Praise can become contempt.
Adoration can become rejection.
If your identity is built on human applause, human rejection will eventually destroy you.
But Paul belonged to Someone deeper than the crowd.
That is why neither worship nor stones could ultimately define him.
And there is something else we must be careful not to miss.
Paul's message to these pagan hearers was not:
“You misunderstood the miracle, but your gods are basically another version of ours.”
No.
He called them away from “vain things” and toward “the living God.”
The Greek word translated “vain” is μάταιος — mataios.
Empty.
Futile.
Powerless to provide what only the living God can give.
Christianity does not announce that humanity simply needs a slightly improved object of inspiration.
The Gospel announces that sinners need reconciliation with the holy God who made them.
And this is where the road eventually leads.
Not to Paul.
Not to Barnabas.
To Jesus Christ.
The apostles were not offering themselves as replacements for pagan gods.
They were witnesses pointing beyond themselves.
Paul's wider preaching makes the center unmistakable: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised.
The Gospel does not say, “Become impressive enough for God.”
It says that the Son of God came for people who could never rescue themselves.
We sinned.
Christ came.
We were guilty.
Christ bore sin.
We were estranged.
Christ opened the way of reconciliation.
We deserved judgment.
Grace came looking for sinners.
And the resurrection announces that death did not get the final word.
That is why the Gospel Warrior theme means so much:
Because Scripture is filled with people whose stories should have ended differently.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul once persecuted the church.
The thief beside Christ was dying under condemnation.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated past.
The prodigal son smelled like the country he had wasted himself in.
And grace kept walking into ruined stories.
Not calling evil good.
Not pretending sin did not matter.
Grace does something far more costly.
Grace confronts sin…
and then points the sinner toward the Savior who paid for it.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending the scandal never happened.
He rewrites everything through redemption.
The scars may remain.
Consequences may remain.
Memories may remain.
But for those who belong to Christ, condemnation does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.

Maybe underneath all the Christian language, church attendance, Bible verses, ministry activity, inspirational posts and carefully constructed smiles, something in you knows there is still an altar that needs to come down.
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe approval.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe money.
Maybe your image.
Maybe a relationship.
Maybe ministry itself.
Maybe you became so consumed with being seen as a person who follows Jesus that you slowly stopped simply following Jesus.
Be honest.
If God removed the applause but left you with Christ…
would Christ still be enough?
That question hurts because idols are rarely exposed while they are starving us.
They are exposed when God asks us to surrender them.
Paul and Barnabas tore their clothes because worship belongs to God.
What needs to be torn away from you?
Not your literal clothing.
The illusion.
The secret throne.
The addiction to approval.
The hunger to be noticed.
The need to control how everybody sees you.
The private compromise you keep defending because surrender feels too expensive.
Jesus did not shed His blood so you could spend your life polishing chains.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is turning from sin and false gods toward the living God.
And the same Gospel that exposes our idols announces mercy to idolaters who come to Christ.
There is forgiveness.
There is grace.
There is cleansing.
There is a new beginning.
Not because your repentance purchases salvation.
Not because tears earn forgiveness.
Salvation is God's gift in Christ.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works so that no one may boast.
And because grace is free, redeemed people become free to live generously—not purchasing God's favor, but responding to mercy already received.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Turn from the idol.
Ask Him for mercy.
Not to perform spirituality.
Not to impress strangers.
Let it simply be your small public confession that you are tired of pretending everything is fine.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only believer fighting in the dark.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God. It does not.
Someone may be addicted to applause.
Someone may have confused Christian celebrity with Christ.
Someone may secretly believe their scandal has disqualified them forever.
Put the Gospel in their path.
Send it privately to the person who disappeared from church.

There may come a day when applause feels intoxicating—or rejection feels unbearable—and you will need to remember two missionaries tearing their clothes in Lystra because they knew the glory was never theirs.
It does not make someone more spiritual.
And God does not need our money.
But supporting Gospel ministry can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership when it is done freely, wisely, and for God's glory.
Never confuse the messenger with the Messiah.
Never give a servant the throne belonging to Jesus.
Paul and Barnabas would rather tear their clothes than steal God's glory.
May God give us Christians who would rather lose followers than replace Christ.
Preachers who would rather become smaller than make Jesus smaller.
Believers who can receive appreciation without turning it into worship.
Ministries courageous enough to say:
Do not build an altar here.
Look beyond us.
Look to Christ.
Because one day every platform disappears.
Every follower count becomes irrelevant.
Every headline is forgotten.
Every human reputation eventually passes from living memory.
But Jesus remains.
The crucified Christ.
The risen Christ.
The reigning Christ.
The Savior of sinners.
The King who does not borrow glory from crowds because all rightful glory already belongs to Him.
So tear down the altar.
Get off the throne.
Stop asking another human being to carry the weight only Jesus can carry.
And if you have spent years chasing applause, hiding scandal, defending sin, or believing your ruined chapters are the end of your story…
come home.
The Gospel is still good news.
Grace is still greater than your résumé.
The cross is still sufficient.
The tomb is still empty.
Jesus is still saving sinners.
And perhaps the greatest thing God could ever do with your name is teach you to spend your life pointing beyond it.
When the crowd tries to make you a god, remember the servants who tore their clothes—and the Savior who willingly had His garments taken from Him as He went to the cross for sinners.
